_about: TerraSync starter knowledge base for Ogun State. DRAFT: written from widely published general practice; every rule is unreviewed, sources are unverified research candidates, and timing windows are approximate. Replace or extend with the Ogun research pack. Schema: backend/app/data/rules.py.

rules.title: Heavy rain is likely in the next few days
rules.action: Clear drainage channels, keep harvested produce covered and off the ground, and avoid spraying anything before rain.
rules.rationale: Waterlogging and wet produce increase crop stress, disease and spoilage.
rules.uncertainty: Forecasts use the Abeokuta location and are approximate for your farm.

rules.title: Little rain expected while your crop is young
rules.action: Check soil moisture. Mulch young plants if you can, and do not sow new seed into dry soil.
rules.rationale: Young crops are most sensitive to dry spells soon after planting.
rules.uncertainty: A short forecast cannot predict the length of a dry spell.

rules.title: Early-season maize planting time
rules.action: Plant once the rains are steady and the soil is moist, not on the first isolated showers.
rules.rationale: A false start to the rains can leave newly planted maize without water.
rules.uncertainty: Southwest Nigeria normally has two rainy seasons (roughly March–July and September–November); onset varies year to year. Check NiMet's seasonal forecast for this year.

rules.title: Late-season maize planting time
rules.action: If planting for the second season, choose an early-maturing variety so the grain fills before the rains end.
rules.rationale: The second rainy season is shorter, so late-maturing varieties risk drought at grain filling.
rules.uncertainty: Southwest Nigeria normally has two rainy seasons (roughly March–July and September–November); onset varies year to year. Check NiMet's seasonal forecast for this year.

rules.title: Keep young maize free of weeds
rules.action: Weed the field during the early weeks after planting, by hoeing or another method you already use safely.
rules.rationale: Young maize competes poorly with weeds for light, water and nutrients.
rules.uncertainty: The 0–6 week window is a broad placeholder; it varies with variety and weed pressure.
rules.contraindications: Avoid deep hoeing close to the plants, which can damage roots.
rules.escalation: Ask an extension officer before using any herbicide.

rules.title: Check maize leaves for fall armyworm
rules.action: Inspect the funnel (whorl) of several plants across the field for ragged holes and sawdust-like droppings.
rules.rationale: Fall armyworm damages young maize quickly; early detection gives more options.
rules.uncertainty: Leaf damage can have other causes. TerraSync cannot confirm a pest from a description.
rules.contraindications: Do not apply pesticides without label instructions and expert advice.
rules.escalation: If you see caterpillars or heavy damage: Contact the Ogun State Agricultural Development Programme (OGADEP) or an extension officer.

rules.title: Get fertiliser advice for your field
rules.action: If you use fertiliser, get the rate and timing for your soil and variety from an extension officer.
rules.rationale: Fertiliser needs depend on soil, previous crop and variety; a single rate does not fit every farm.
rules.uncertainty: TerraSync does not give fertiliser rates.
rules.escalation: Contact the Ogun State Agricultural Development Programme (OGADEP) or an extension officer.

rules.title: Check whether your maize is ready to harvest
rules.action: Look for dry, brown husks and hard grain. Prepare bags, labour and a clean drying surface before harvesting.
rules.rationale: Harvesting at maturity and drying promptly reduces mould and storage losses.
rules.uncertainty: Maturity depends strongly on variety; the window shown is approximate.
rules.contraindications: Do not leave mature maize in the field for long during rainy periods.

rules.title: Rain is forecast during your harvest period
rules.action: Plan harvesting around dry days and keep harvested cobs or grain covered and off the ground.
rules.rationale: Wet grain is more likely to develop mould during drying and storage.
rules.uncertainty: Forecasts are approximate and use the Abeokuta location, not your farm.

rules.title: Dry maize well before storing it
rules.action: Dry shelled grain thoroughly, store it in clean, airtight bags off the floor, and check regularly for insects.
rules.rationale: Moist grain and storage insects are major causes of post-harvest loss.
rules.uncertainty: TerraSync cannot measure grain moisture; use a moisture meter or local test if available.
rules.contraindications: Do not mix new grain with old, infested grain.

rules.title: Sort out mouldy or damaged maize
rules.action: Remove mouldy, insect-damaged or broken cobs and grain before storage or sale, and never dry maize on bare soil.
rules.rationale: Mould on maize can produce aflatoxins, which are harmful and reduce market value.
rules.uncertainty: Aflatoxin cannot be seen; sorting reduces but does not remove the risk.

rules.title: Tell buyers about your coming maize harvest
rules.action: Report your expected quantity and date on the TerraSync produce board so buyers can plan ahead.
rules.rationale: Buyers and aggregators can arrange collection earlier when they know supply is coming.
rules.uncertainty: Interest on the board is not a guaranteed sale.

rules.title: Cassava planting time
rules.action: Plant cassava cuttings when the soil is moist after the rains have started.
rules.rationale: Cuttings need soil moisture to sprout and root well.
rules.uncertainty: Southwest Nigeria normally has two rainy seasons (roughly March–July and September–November); onset varies year to year. Check NiMet's seasonal forecast for this year.

rules.title: Use cuttings from healthy cassava plants
rules.action: Take stems only from healthy, mature plants without yellow, twisted leaves, and plant them soon after cutting.
rules.rationale: Diseases such as cassava mosaic spread through infected cuttings.
rules.uncertainty: A healthy-looking plant can still carry disease; certified planting material is safer where available.
rules.escalation: Ask OGADEP about sources of improved, clean cassava stems.

rules.title: Keep young cassava weeded
rules.action: Weed regularly in the first months after planting until the leaves cover the ground.
rules.rationale: Cassava grows slowly at first, so early weed competition can greatly reduce root yield.
rules.uncertainty: The 0–3 month window is a broad placeholder.
rules.contraindications: Avoid damaging the stems and shallow roots while weeding.
rules.escalation: Ask an extension officer before using any herbicide.

rules.title: Look for yellow, twisted cassava leaves
rules.action: Check leaves for yellow-green mottling or twisting. Mark affected plants and do not use them for cuttings.
rules.rationale: Mosaic-type diseases spread through infected cuttings and whiteflies and can reduce yield.
rules.uncertainty: Leaf symptoms are not a diagnosis; nutrient problems can look similar.
rules.escalation: If many plants are affected: Contact the Ogun State Agricultural Development Programme (OGADEP) or an extension officer.

rules.title: Plan cassava harvest around processing or sale
rules.action: Arrange processing, transport or a buyer before you uproot, and harvest only what can be handled quickly.
rules.rationale: Cassava roots keep in the ground but spoil quickly once harvested.
rules.uncertainty: Maturity varies widely by variety; the window shown is approximate.

rules.title: Process or sell harvested cassava quickly
rules.action: Move harvested roots to processing or buyers as soon as possible and avoid bruising or cutting them.
rules.rationale: Fresh cassava roots start to deteriorate within a few days of harvest.
rules.uncertainty: Shelf life depends on handling and conditions.

rules.title: Tell processors about your cassava
rules.action: Report the quantity you expect to harvest and when, so processors can plan collection before you uproot.
rules.rationale: Matching harvest to processor demand reduces losses from roots waiting after harvest.
rules.uncertainty: Interest on the board is not a guaranteed sale.

rules.title: Yam planting time
rules.action: Plant healthy setts on prepared mounds or ridges early in the rainy season.
rules.rationale: Early planting gives yam the full rainy season to grow tubers.
rules.uncertainty: Southwest Nigeria normally has two rainy seasons (roughly March–July and September–November); onset varies year to year. Check NiMet's seasonal forecast for this year. Some farmers plant late in the dry season with mulch; ask locally.

rules.title: Use clean, healthy yam setts
rules.action: Choose setts from firm tubers without rot, cracks or insect damage.
rules.rationale: Rot and pests on planting material reduce sprouting and spread to the new crop.
rules.uncertainty: Visual checks cannot detect all diseases.

rules.title: Stake your yam vines
rules.action: Provide stakes or trellises so vines climb and leaves get sunlight.
rules.rationale: Staked yam vines usually capture more light, which supports tuber growth.
rules.uncertainty: The benefit varies with variety and site; the timing shown is approximate.

rules.title: Keep yam mounds weeded
rules.action: Weed around mounds regularly, taking care not to damage vines or expose tubers.
rules.rationale: Weeds compete with young yam for water and nutrients.
rules.uncertainty: Timing is approximate.

rules.title: Check whether your yam is ready
rules.action: When most leaves and vines turn yellow and dry, dig carefully to avoid cutting or bruising the tubers.
rules.rationale: Damaged tubers rot quickly in storage.
rules.uncertainty: Maturity depends on variety and planting time; the window shown is approximate.

rules.title: Store yam in a shaded, airy place
rules.action: Handle tubers gently, keep them in a well-ventilated, shaded barn or rack, and remove rotting tubers regularly.
rules.rationale: Heat, poor airflow and wounds speed up rotting and sprouting.
rules.uncertainty: Storage life varies by variety and conditions.

rules.title: Stake tomatoes and check for disease
rules.action: Stake plants to keep fruit off the soil, and check for wilting or spotted leaves. Remove badly affected plants.
rules.rationale: Tomato is very prone to leaf and soil-borne diseases, especially in wet weather.
rules.uncertainty: Days are counted from transplanting. Symptoms are not a diagnosis.
rules.contraindications: Do not spray without label instructions and expert advice.
rules.escalation: If plants wilt suddenly or many leaves are spotted: Contact the Ogun State Agricultural Development Programme (OGADEP) or an extension officer.

rules.title: Wet weather raises tomato disease risk
rules.action: Improve airflow by pruning crowded leaves, avoid working among wet plants, and harvest ripe fruit before heavy rain.
rules.rationale: Diseases spread faster on wet leaves; rain also splits ripening fruit.
rules.uncertainty: Forecasts are approximate for your farm.

rules.title: Harvest tomatoes at colour change for transport
rules.action: Pick fruit as it starts to change colour if it must travel, and fully red fruit only for nearby sale.
rules.rationale: Fruit picked at colour change survives transport better.
rules.uncertainty: Days are counted from transplanting and vary by variety.

rules.title: Pack tomatoes in crates, not sacks
rules.action: Use shallow crates or baskets, keep them in shade, and do not overfill or stack fruit too deep.
rules.rationale: Crushing in sacks and heat are major causes of tomato losses between farm and market.
rules.uncertainty: Loss levels vary with distance and handling.

rules.title: Line up buyers before your tomatoes ripen
rules.action: Report expected quantity and picking dates on the produce board so buyers can plan collection.
rules.rationale: Tomatoes cannot wait long after harvest, so early coordination reduces waste.
rules.uncertainty: Interest on the board is not a guaranteed sale.

rules.title: Check pepper plants for pests and disease
rules.action: Look under leaves for insects and check for curled, spotted or wilting leaves. Remove badly affected plants.
rules.rationale: Early detection limits spread through the field.
rules.uncertainty: Days are counted from transplanting. Symptoms are not a diagnosis.
rules.escalation: Contact the Ogun State Agricultural Development Programme (OGADEP) or an extension officer.

rules.title: Pick peppers regularly
rules.action: Harvest mature fruit every few days, cutting or twisting gently so branches are not broken.
rules.rationale: Regular picking reduces over-ripe and damaged fruit.
rules.uncertainty: Days are counted from transplanting and vary by variety.

rules.title: Dry peppers on a clean, raised surface
rules.action: If drying, spread peppers thinly on mats or raised racks, turn them often and cover them from rain and dew.
rules.rationale: Drying on bare ground and rewetting lead to mould and dirt contamination.
rules.uncertainty: Drying time depends on weather.

rules.title: Weed groundnut early
rules.action: Weed during the first weeks, then avoid disturbing the soil once pegs start entering the ground.
rules.rationale: Early weeds reduce yield; late disturbance damages developing pods.
rules.uncertainty: Timing is approximate.

rules.title: Check whether groundnuts are ready
rules.action: Pull a few plants: most pods should have a darkened inner shell and well-filled kernels. Lift when the soil is not waterlogged.
rules.rationale: Harvesting too early lowers yield; too late increases pod loss in the soil.
rules.uncertainty: Maturity depends on variety; the window shown is approximate.

rules.title: Dry groundnuts quickly and sort them
rules.action: Dry pods off the ground soon after lifting, then remove damaged, shrivelled or mouldy pods before storage.
rules.rationale: Slow drying and damaged pods raise the risk of aflatoxin contamination.
rules.uncertainty: Aflatoxin cannot be seen; sorting reduces but does not remove the risk.

maize.uncertainty: Early-maturing varieties can be ready sooner; late varieties later.

cassava.uncertainty: Cassava can be harvested over a long period; choose timing by variety and market.

yam.uncertainty: Depends on variety and planting date.

tomato.uncertainty: Picking continues for several weeks once it starts.

pepper.uncertainty: Picking continues for several weeks once it starts.
